{{Short description|Theorem in probability theory}}
The '''Hewitt–Savage zero–one law''' is a [[theorem]] in [[probability theory]], similar to [[Kolmogorov's zero–one law]] and the [[Borel–Cantelli lemma]], that specifies that a certain type of event will either [[almost surely]] happen or almost surely not happen. It is sometimes known as the '''Savage-Hewitt law for symmetric events'''. It is named after [[Edwin Hewitt]] and [[Leonard Jimmie Savage]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Hewitt | first1 = E. | authorlink1 = Edwin Hewitt | last2=Savage | first2=L. J. | authorlink2=Leonard Jimmie Savage | title = Symmetric measures on Cartesian products | journal = Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. | volume = 80 | year = 1955 | pages = 470–501 | doi=10.1090/s0002-9947-1955-0076206-8 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

==Statement of the Hewitt-Savage zero-one law==
Let <math>\left\{ X_n \right\}_{n = 1}^\infty</math> be a [[sequence]] of [[independent and identically distributed random variables]] taking values in a set <math>\mathbb{X}</math>.  The Hewitt-Savage zero–one law says that any event whose occurrence or non-occurrence is determined by the values of these random variables and whose occurrence or non-occurrence is unchanged by finite [[permutation]]s of the indices, has [[probability]] either 0 or 1 (a “finite” permutation is one that leaves all but finitely many of the indices fixed).

Somewhat more abstractly, define the [[Invariant sigma-algebra#Exchangeable sigma algebra|exchangeable sigma algebra]] or ''sigma algebra of symmetric events'' <math>\mathcal{E}</math> to be the set of events (depending on the sequence of variables <math>\left\{ X_n \right\}_{n = 1}^\infty</math>) which are invariant under [[Wikt:finite|finite]] [[permutation]]s of the indices in the sequence <math>\left\{ X_n \right\}_{n = 1}^\infty</math>. Then <math>A \in \mathcal{E} \implies \mathbb{P} (A) \in \{ 0, 1 \}</math>.

Since any finite permutation can be written as a product of [[transposition (mathematics)|transposition]]s, if we wish to check whether or not an event <math>A</math> is symmetric (lies in <math>\mathcal{E}</math>), it is enough to check if its occurrence is unchanged by an arbitrary transposition <math>(i, j)</math>, <math>i, j \in \mathbb{N}</math>.

==Example==

Let the sequence <math>\left\{ X_n \right\}_{n = 1}^\infty</math> of independent and identically distributed random variables taking values in <math>\R</math>. Consider the random walk <math>S_N= \sum_{n = 1}^N X_n</math>. Then one of the following occurs with probability 1:
* <math>S_N=0</math>
* <math>S_N\to\infty</math>
* <math>S_N\to-\infty</math>
* <math>\liminf S_N = -\infty</math> and <math>\limsup S_N = \infty</math>.

Since ''S''<sub>''N''</sub> are not independent the [[Kolmogorov's zero–one law]] is not directly applicable.

First consider the case when ''X''<sub>''1''</sub> is a.s. constant. Then with probability 1 we have that either (<math>S_N=0</math>), (<math>S_N\to\infty</math>) or (<math>S_N\to-\infty</math>).

Now consider the case, when ''X''<sub>''1''</sub> is not a.s. constant. Then for any <math>t\in[-\infty,\infty]</math> the event <math>\left\{\limsup S_N\geq t \right\}</math> is in the exchangeable sigma algebra. That is because [[limit supremum]] does not change with finite permutation of the indices. From Hewitt-Savage zero-one law we have that
:<math>\mathbb{P}\left(\limsup S_N\geq t \right) \in \{0,1\}</math>.
There has to exist ''t'', where probability switches from 0 to 1 i.e. exists <math>t^*\in[-\infty,\infty]</math> such that <math>\limsup S_n = t^*</math> almost surely. Similarly exists <math>t_*\in[-\infty,\infty]</math> such that <math>\liminf S_n = t_*</math> almost surely.

Since almost surely
:<math>t^*=\limsup S_N = X_1 + \limsup \sum_{n = 2}^N X_n=X_1+t^*</math>
and ''X''<sub>''1''</sub> is not a.s. 0, then <math>t^*</math> is not finite. Similarly <math>t_*</math> in not finite.

Therefore, with probability 1 either (<math>S_N\to\infty</math>), (<math>S_N\to-\infty</math>)
or (<math>\liminf S_N = -\infty</math> and <math>\limsup S_N = \infty</math>).<ref>This example is from {{cite web
 | title=Hewitt–Savage 0–1 application
 | website=Mathematics Stack Exchange
 | date=12 January 2020
 | url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/3506143/hewitt-savage-0-text-1-application
 | access-date=19 November 2025
}}</ref>
